analysis.one_liner: Lets local regulators cap basic cable rates and lets phone companies compete with cable.
analysis.headline: The Cable Competition Act was introduced in the Senate in May 1989 with six cosponsors from both parties, but it never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responds to cable bills that kept climbing after the cable industry was deregulated. It would let state or local franchising authorities cap rates for a basic 'lifeline' TV package — network channels, public TV, and local stations — in areas where only one cable company operates. It would repeal the ban on telephone companies offering video service in their own service areas, with FCC rules meant to keep phone ratepayers from footing the bill for the new ventures. It would also force cable systems to carry unaffiliated programming on the same terms as programming owned by the cable company itself, and order federal investigations into cable industry concentration, pricing, and rural TV access.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers in monopoly franchise areas, who could see a basic lifeline tier regulated; competing program producers and alternative distributors, who would get guaranteed access to cable systems; telephone companies, which could enter the video business; and rural households, whose access to television service would get a dedicated federal study.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cable subscribers and rival video providers

how_it_helps.text: In any franchise area served by fewer than two cable operators, states or local franchising authorities could regulate rates for a lifeline television tier consisting of the three major networks, a public TV station, and each local independent station [S2][S3].

The bill repeals the Communications Act provision prohibiting telephone companies from providing video programming in their service areas, letting them offer video directly or through affiliates, subject to FCC rules protecting basic telephone ratepayers from cross-subsidies [S2][S3].

Cable operators would have to give any qualifying program service access to their systems, and unaffiliated program services would get the same rates, terms, and conditions as services owned by the cable operator — aimed at cable companies using their control of the wire to favor their own channels [S2][S3].

The bill makes it unlawful for any company affiliated with a cable operator that provides programming to discriminate unreasonably against a rival seeking that programming for another cable system or another delivery medium [S2][S3].

The FTC would investigate whether cable-affiliated programmers raise rates or engage in anticompetitive practices, and whether large multiple-system operators buy systems at inflated prices that drive a spiral of rate increases; the FCC would study how to extend video service to rural areas [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable operators would face rate regulation in monopoly areas, mandatory carriage of unaffiliated channels, and nondiscrimination rules that limit the profits from owning both the wire and the programming. Telephone companies would bear the investment risk of new video ventures, shielded from shifting losses onto phone ratepayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Cable operators and, initially, phone companies

drawbacks.text: The rate cap applies only to a basic lifeline tier in areas without two competing cable operators, leaving most expanded-tier pricing unregulated — a narrow remedy for the 'significantly higher consumer rates' the bill itself cites as the problem [S3].

Opening the video market to telephone companies could substitute one dominant provider for another, and the bill's own FCC rules (separating telephone ratepayers from video-business risk) acknowledge that cross-subsidy was a real hazard [S3].
The main enforcement provisions depend on future FCC regulations and on FTC and FCC studies with one-year reporting deadlines, so consumers would see no benefit until regulators acted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's consumer protections are real but modest — a rate cap on a bare-bones tier, plus competition that might lower prices over time — and its strongest tools are largely studies and future rulemaking. The clearest immediate winners besides subscribers are the telephone companies gaining entry to a new market. On balance the costs fall mainly on cable operators who had been earning monopoly-level rates without competitive pressure.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee in May 1989 and nothing further ever happened; it died there when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Albert Gore Jr. introduced the bill with Senators Slade Gorton and Wendell Ford on May 18, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S3][S5].
Six senators cosponsored the bill — three Republicans and three Democrats [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind after the referral; the Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable operators, which kept unregulated rates in monopoly areas and continued controlling which programming reached their systems. Telephone companies remained barred from offering video service, so their potential gain died with the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable operators kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a bipartisan original team — a Democrat from Tennessee, a Republican from Washington, and a Democrat from Kentucky — and its six cosponsors split evenly, three Republicans and three Democrats [S4].

industries.note: The bill caps lifeline-tier rates in monopoly areas, mandates carriage of unaffiliated channels on equal terms, and bars affiliated programmers from discriminating against rivals. Cable operators had been earning rising rates without competition since deregulation, and the bill's own findings say so [S3].

The bill repeals the ban on telephone companies delivering video programming in their own service areas, opening a large new market. Its entry was framed as pro-consumer competition, with FCC rules to keep phone ratepayers from subsidizing it [S2][S3].

Programmers owned by or affiliated with cable operators would face a prohibition on unjust or unreasonable discrimination against rivals seeking their programming for other systems, undercutting their gatekeeper position [S3].

The bill's findings say new distribution technologies benefit consumers, especially in rural areas, but need fair access to programming; the nondiscrimination rules would extend to programming sought for delivery over other media [S3].
